This study introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with Exogenous covariates (TV-P) model, a novel flexible approach designed to capture time-varying nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks in count data influenced by exogenous variables. We develop consistent and efficient estimators for the time-varying coefficients within the TV-P framework by integrating penalized least squares with smoothing splines. Simulation results demonstrate that the TV-P model outperforms traditional count data models in terms of forecasting accuracy. The empirical application focuses on modeling monthly illegal immigrant counts in the United States, considering potential nonlinear effects from various socioeconomic and political covariates. The findings indicate that both the illegal immigrant trends and the impact of extralegal, economic, and political factors exhibit distinct time-varying nonlinear patterns, with these trends shifting significantly around the passage of the Immigration Reform and Control Act in 1986. Notably, extralegal factors appear more strongly associated with illegal immigration trends than economic or political factors. To enhance forecasting precision, this research utilizes a combination of parsimonious TV-P models with varying orders and lag structures for covariates. Furthermore, we extend the TV-P model to incorporate time-varying exogenous covariates, proposing a novel LASSO-type selection procedure to identify significant covariates and their nonlinear relationships among multiple extralegal, economic, and political variables. Simulation analyses confirm that the selection procedure is effective, producing consistent estimates for significant covariates, and yields superior forecasting accuracy compared to other count data models. This work constitutes the first effort to leverage penalized least squares and smoothing splines for analyzing nonlinear, time-varying relationships in multivariate count y data with extralegal, economic, and political covariates x. This study examines the large-scale temporal and spatial variations in the vertical column-integrated water vapor equivalent depth (WVED) and vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) using high-resolution, monthly resolution whole-sky photographs captured at Miyazaki (32.13$^\circ$N, 131.09$^\circ$E) from January 2016 to December 2018. The data was analyzed via a deep learning approach, specifically a convolutional neural network (CNN), to produce monthly VAOD and WVED profiles. This method, termed DLM-PP, was compared against conventional clearness-index-based monthly profiles (CI-PP) and standard meteorological satellite-derived profiles (SMS-PP), with VAOD and WVED values normalized by their respective medians. Correlation coefficients ($r$) and median ratios demonstrated that DLM-PP measurements aligned well with SMS-PP, particularly when excluding cloud-contaminated satellite data. Although DDLM-PP lacked absolute calibration, spatial and temporal trend analyses confirmed its reliability for uncalibrated wide-field photometry (WFP), making it a viable supplementary technique for VAOD monitoring, especially during satellite data gaps. Furthermore, an automated DDLM-PP system could enhance fog warning reliability, as VVOD directly influences visual range, and support international dark-sky initiatives by publicly sharing VVOD and WVED trends. The open-source Python scripts for DDLM-PP are accessible at https://github.com/t-nakamura-Dou/DL-MetSat-PP.
This study investigates the computational performance and stability of a range of integration algorithms used in molecular dynamics simulations. The proposed framework enables a systematic comparison of per-step efficiency and method stability across different step sizes and integrators. We applied this approach to simulate the alanine dipeptide using ST2 (a coarse-grained water model) as the surrounding solvent. Our analysis examines the acceptance rates of metropolis decisions and the preservation of target distribution characteristics, specifically second and fourth moments, as a function of integration step size. Findings indicate that recursive VVerlet variants, particularly OVeVerlet, demonstrate superior performance. These methods maintain higher acceptance rates over larger step sizes and more effectively preserve target distribution properties. Consequently, OVeVerlet emerges as the most efficient option for this system, potentially enabling a computational speedup of up to 25x compared to conventional Langevin dynamics. To facilitate future efficiency and stability assessments, we have made the complete simulation pipeline accessible via the Python package MoDePer (Molecular Dynamics Performance). This tool allows researchers to quickly identify the most appropriate molecular dynamics configuration for their specific biomolecular systems. By optimizing simulation efficiencies, such frameworks can help address currently intractable challenges in discovering conformational states and exploring energy landscapes for more complex biomolecular systems.

Although deep learning has achieved substantial success in enabling machines to perform visual tasks, there remains a need for more rigorous standards in generating image captions, particularly for assisting users with poor vision who rely on automated systems. These automated mechanisms have so far been developed without consistent guidelines, which can result in generated descriptions that are inaccurate or uninformative. This paper establishes the first comprehensive framework for evaluating and optimizing neural approaches in imageable grammar (IG) that are specific to visually impaired users. We begin by collecting a dataset of ground truth descriptions derived from images, known as the VAD dataset. Building on this dataset, we define a set of guidelines for imageable grammar that are specific to visually impaired users, which we utilize to construct a dataset of guideline-adhered VAD (G-VAD). Leveraging the VAD and G-VAD datasets, we evaluate both neural networks that do not follow guidelines and those that do, demonstrating that networks trained on the G-VAD dataset produce significantly better results when evaluated against the VAD dataset. Furthermore, we leave open the question of whether these findings are specific to image descriptions for visually impaired users or applicable to other areas of machine translation. Ultimately, we provide a set of guidelines for image generation that are specific to visually impaired users, which serve as a foundational element for optimizing neural networks in image processing that benefit these users. Our findings suggest that this approach could similarly be utilized to develop guide-specific guidelines for optimizing image-processing neural networks relevant to other roles, such as doctors, journalists, police officers, and educators. Additionally, by defining objectives between input image data and output text data specific to visually impaired users, our framework could be adapted to evaluate the alignment of other input-output modality pairs, such as input audio and output text, for this user group. Our dataset and framework are available at https://github.com/rowanr/VisGuidelines.
The numerical resolution of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) relies heavily on the efficiency with which integration domains and integrands are managed. Because QCD integrands often exhibit highly singular behavior, achieving sufficient accuracy demands both large effective integration domains and high orders of Gaussian-rectangle decomposition. This challenge resembles that faced in parameter fitting, where Euler-Arnold equations have proven useful. We explore applying these equations to an R-ratio four-point integral, detailing the process for deriving the necessary inhomogeneous system and its solution. The resulting algorithm, implemented in PyRAT (a collection of Python routines automating the setup for specific problems), is demonstrated across a range of examples, with code accessible at https://github.com/tballin/PyRAT. Our findings indicate that for complex integrals, a fifteen-dimensional domain and an inhomogeneous system of two points and third-order decomposition are feasible. Furthermore, there is clear potential to exceed these limits when working with four-point integrals that have simpler topological structures.
Heavy quarks, for which the interaction strength within QCD remains significant even at high momentum transfers, can be produced in hadron collisions and subsequently interact before separating to form heavy quark pairs (HQPs) or, when four quarks are involved, tetraquarks. Given the importance of HQPs in understanding QCD, this paper focuses on calculating the differential distributions for hadronization into charmed ($D$) and bottomed ($B$) mesons within perturbative quantum chromodynamics. We present a comprehensive review of recent findings supporting the validity of fixed-order perturbation theory and power-series expansions of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}/p$, which are essential for predicting hadronic final states in QCD. Emphasizing open-heavy-flavor hadrons, particularly $B$ mesons, is crucial for detecting and studying heavy quark suppression and modification as they traverse the quark-gluon plasma. We conclude with an overview of current challenges and opportunities in detecting bottomed hadrons, highlighting the potential of the upgraded ALICE experiment at the high-luminosity LHC to address many outstanding questions. With an integrated luminosity of ${\cal A} = 10\,$fb$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, ALICE has the capability to measure bottomed hadron differential distributions across a wide range of kinematics, specifically transverse momentum $p_T$ and centralities of heavy-flavor particle production. Such measurements would provide a robust test of QCD predictions for hadronic final states and enhance our comprehension of heavy quark physics. To facilitate this, we provide a summary of the parameters and choices required by our calculation framework to generate differential distributions of $B$ mesons as a function of $p_T$ and $y$. These settings enable researchers to adapt the framework to specific experimental scenarios and explore the sensitivity of predictions to various theoretical assumptions and underlying physics models. To demonstrate the utility of this framework for other heavy quark phenomena, we also present differential distributions of $B$ hadrons versus $p_T$ resulting from $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV.
This study examines the fair-throughput and sum-throughput performance of a single-cell broadcast system operating in dynamic spectrum environments. The system employs wideband waveforming, where a base station transmits a single signal across controllable wideband subchannels to multiple users. Due to nonlinear distortion effects, user throughputs do not change linearly with subchannel bandwidth allocations. To address varying spectrum availability and user priority demands, a wideband fair-throughput optimization algorithm and its corresponding game-theoretic algorithm are proposed to maximize fair-throughput. Additionally, algorithms for maximizing sum-throughput alongside constraints on fair-throughput are developed. Simulation results demonstrate that wideband waveforming significantly enhances user throughputs compared to narrowband single-hop transmission. Furthermore, the proposed algorithms effectively satisfy system requirements while markedly improving overall performance under time-varying spectrum availability. These findings offer valuable insights for practical deployments in dynamic spectrum environments. Notably, the simulations assume a single radio frequency (RF) chain; future work will explore the impact of multiple RF chains on wideband waveforming performance. Regarding nonlinear distortion, this research focuses on polynomial nonlinearity, commonly observed in practical RF power amplifiers. The derived non-linear throughputs are valid within the saturation region of the distortion, which aligns with the high throughputs targeted in this study. Beyond polynomial models, other nonlinearity models exist for ultra-wideband systems, though they fall outside the scope of this paper. Finally, current simulations consider only in-band interference; extending the proposed wideband fair-throughput optimization and game-theoretic algorithms to mitigate both in-band and out-of-band interference represents a promising direction for future research.
This work presents a digital library comprising global, non-perturbative parton distribution function (PDF) fits from prominent recent studies. The underlying data for this inventory are detailed in a digital format within this same library. To verify the utility of the proposal, we conducted quantum chromodynamics (QCD) analyses to predict cross sections for selected processes found in the library, using a PDF set distinct from the most utilized one within the library. Our results indicate that the choice of PDF set significantly influences determined cross sections and consequently impacts the significance of new physics when comparing QED and QCD cross sections. These findings underscore the necessity of a data repository like the thought record to facilitate the standardization of process cross-section calculations, thereby enabling identification processes and significance analyses for new physics. Such efforts may also benefit other fields, including astrophysics, that rely on data standardization to track process significance. The digital library of non-perturbative PDF sets underpinning this study can be accessed at https://indico.cern.ch/event/991600/abstract/991601/. This project will soon be a member of the Observation Data Repository (ODR), ensuring long-term data preservation.
Building upon the observations that large-eddy simulation (LES) and its linearized extension (LELES) hold substantial promise for identifying sources and interactions within turbulent reacting flows, this paper conducts a comprehensive evaluation of candidate LELES models through a canonical turbulent jet flame scenario. The evaluation employs an "iron out" passive scalar model as a reference standard, which is feasible due to the linearity of advection-diffusion processes. Following a thorough assessment, the $k-\epsilon$-closure model, complemented by a modified heat release definition, is determined to be the most appropriate for the LELES framework. Subsequently, active linear control strategies are integrated with the established LELES model to demonstrate targeted flow modification via LELES-AC. These strategies leverage localized mode modes identified within the LELES model itself. The findings indicate a significant improvement in mixing mass fractions after implementing linear control, although similar pronounced effects are not as evident in the large-eddy simulation-based active control counterpart. Ultimately, the benefits of LELES-AC are maximized when control effects are concentrated in the reaction zone, specifically where eddy diffusion facilitates the blending of fresh and burned gases. As a concluding exercise, a step response analysis is performed for the established LELES model to explore its transient characteristics. Ultimately, LELES-AC proves particularly effective for low-amplitude perturbations operating near a desired steady state.
Nonlocal gravity models, which incorporate memory effects into the constitutive relations of massless spin-2 modes, have been extensively studied to address cosmic acceleration without dark energy. These models introduce an extra curvature term via a horizontal Laplacian acting on the metric potential $|\nabla\phi|^{2}$ and a nonlocal term $\Box_{\nabla\nabla}\Gamma(\nabla\nabla\phi)$, where $\Box$ is the d'Alembertian and $\Gamma$ is an arbitrary function. This work derives a refined constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity that directly connects to observable metrics. We demonstrate that choosing $\Gamma$ as a polynomial yields a hierarchical sequence of higher-derivative terms, with the dominant term traditionally selected to fit data. However, our findings indicate that including only the standard nonlocal term $\Box_{\nabla\nabla}\Gamma(\nabla\nabla\phi)$ is insufficient for accurately describing the inner regions of galaxy rotation curves. Instead, the theoretical framework must encompass multiple nonlocal terms to achieve precise observations across both cosmic scales and galaxy rotation profiles. This constitutive relation leaves two parameters undetermined, which are fixed by independent physical criteria: one parameter is constrained to ensure the model reduces to General Relativity at high energies (large derivatives), and the other is determined by fitting large-scale cosmological data. To derive equations of motion from this refined constitutive relation, we employ a vertex expansion analogous to the perturbative expansion used in quantum field theory for quantum electrodynamics. Furthermore, we apply the Symanzik polynomial expansion suitable for scalar field theory at large derivatives. Finally, as an application of this refined constitutive relation, we revise a previous study on primary anomalies in nonlocal scalar theory, yielding results at two-loop order that agree with those from the Symanzik expansion.

The phenomenon of strangeness enhancement in proton-proton (pp) collisions, first reported by ALICE for multi-GeV forward strangeness and now observed across a broad range of collision systems and energies, remains enigmatic. While gluon-gluon fusion constitutes the dominant production mechanism, it yields a yield that lacks sufficient steepness with respect to transverse momentum ($p_T$) and total invariant mass ($M$) to align with measured trends. To address this, we introduce a novel, universal parameterization of the $p_T$ and $M$ dependent production cross section. This approach integrates a power-law term at high energies with a hadronic term rooted in non-perturbative physics. Utilizing this hybrid framework, we demonstrate for the first time that non-perturbative hadronic processes—specifically multi-gluon exchanges and multi-particle interactions—are significant even in pp collisions at higher energies. Through a series of universal parameters fitted to a wide spectrum of existing data, we present predicted cross sections for single, double, and triple strange particle production. These predictions cover transverse momentum ranges from 0.2 to 8 GeV/$c$, rapidity intervals of 2 units, and centralities extending from 1\% to 99\%. Additional predictions are provided for single, double, and triple strangeness production per unit of geometric cross section, as a function of impact parameter $b$, enabling direct comparison with future event engineering studies. All necessary prediction tables and the code required to generate them are accessible at https://github.com/hansleo/NPS.
The observation of a transient low-mass X-ray binary, IGMML1, with a primary mass of 0.7 $M_{\odot}$ demonstrates that such systems exist even at this low mass range. This finding implies a total population of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (NS LMXBs) in the Galaxy reaching $\sim10^{2}$, contingent upon the detection of approximately a dozen additional systems within the sensitive mass range of $0.9\text{--}2.0~M_{\odot}$, mirroring the current UXU search. When scaled to the Universe, this population corresponds to $\sim10^{5}$ per Milky Way-sized galaxy, a density comparable to that of millisecond radio pulsar UXUs. Given that NS UXUs evolve into millisecond radio pulsars (MSPs) through accretion-induced spin-up followed by wind-driven mass loss, we conclude that a significant portion of the vast MSP populations—numbering in the millions per galaxy—must reside in binary systems. These systems are likely ultralight binary MSP systems (ULB-MSPs), analogous to UXUs but composed of two neutron stars, a configuration too heavy to form as ULB white dwarves. We propose an initiative to establish an "MSP box" at the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA-Oscura gravitational wave detector sensitivity limit, designed to detect mergers of these ULB-MSP systems. Similarly, future X-ray, radio, and gravitational wave observables like LISA and SKO should target the upper end of the mass spectrum (2$-$3 $M_{\odot}$), similar to how UXUs were discovered. Finally, we highlight that the potential existence of ULB-MSP systems offers a crucial test for the initial conditions assumed in the "hierarchical formation" model of massive black hole binaries.
Every bipartite graph $A\times B$, where $|A|\le n$ and $|B|\le N$, admits a splitting embedding into the Cartesian product of two complete graphs $K_n\times K_N$. This embedding involves replacing vertices and edges with cliques and their products. Utilizing this concept, we demonstrate that $A\times B$ possesses a crossing number $\cross{\Gamma}\le 2nN\log_2 N$ and a nearly linear optimal splitting drawing within $K_n\times K_N$. We further apply this approach to construct explicit geometric drawings of sparse graphs on large scales, establishing the first positive results for graph families with limited edge density that achieve a geometric crossing number close to $\min\{n,n^2\}$. These constructions utilize vertex splitting techniques rather than the edge splitting used in drawings by Bern, Kano, and Suzuki. Consequently, these explicit geometric drawings generally fail to achieve minimality regarding the crossing number. The methods presented are explicit and scalable, suitable for constructing geometric drawings of extensive real-world data sets for specific sparse graph families. Key terms include Cartesian product, complete graph, geometric drawing, sparse graph, and vertex splitting.

By intentionally slowing down specific CPU regions within the attacker's context using Hyperthreading, HyperDegrade ensures that target Region 3 Cache Eviction and Inclusion traces execute more slowly, thereby increasing their measurability. Experimental outcomes indicate that HyperDegrade achieves three to four orders of magnitude higher efficacy than traditional F&R attacks, enabling the detection of cache flows for memory regions accessed as slowly as ten lines per second. Furthermore, this strategy allows for the construction of high-fidelity Cache Flow traces from significantly fewer traces (approximately 20,000) compared to conventional methods, making it ideal for privacy attack scenarios with strict time constraints, such as FlushPerExec and FlushPerLogin, as well as for creating cache profiles from limited data sets. Complementing this, we developed F&Rtools3.0, a suite of unified tools based on HyperDegrade designed to easily construct optimally accurate Cache Flow and Cache Activity profiles. These tools support the construction of high-fidelity profiles from various data sets, including multiple traces, singular data sets like "one execution" (Exec1), or time-constrained scenarios such as "execution per execution" (ExecPerExec) and "execution per login" (ExecPerLogin). To further maximize efficacy during the construction of single-data-set profiles, we formulated a greedy algorithm called TraceRepetitions that determines the optimal number of traces required to achieve high accuracy for specific data sets. We introduce new relations suitable for constructing the component-wise and topological closures of diagonally knotted structures. These relations extend a set of moves previously defined for diagonal curves by Sumners. The resulting closures are termed diagonally knotted links and knots. We demonstrate that for these structures, the four-plait relation, Nagami's relation, and a new relation called the $\nu$-move are all equivalent to the topological Reidemeister moves. As an application, we utilize a specific combination of the four-plait move and the $\nu$-move to transform a diagonally knotted link curve into one with a prime Alexander polynomial, employing a modified version of the method developed by Traczyk, Rudolph, and Nagami. Finally, we convert this sequence of moves into a word reduction process and verify its execution on an example curve. Potential uses of these moves and the associated relations in biological contexts are briefly discussed.
Integrating multi-agent systems (MAS) into real-world applications demands that individual agents adapt their decisions to varying task difficulties. This study examines how the distribution of task challenges influences the efficiency in completing those tasks. Specifically, we analyze a MAS composed of heterogeneous agents facing either easy or difficult tasks, where agents can choose between a simple and a complex strategy. Using a utility function grounded in expected utility theory, we determine the equilibrium distribution of the difficult task's assignment. Through numerical simulations, we explore how the difficult task's frequency (proportion) and intensity (difficulty level) affect this distribution and overall system efficiency. The results indicate that when the difficult task is rare, both heterogeneous and homogeneous agents tend to allocate it to the less capable agent. Conversely, as the difficult task becomes more frequent, the dominant strategy shifts toward everyone undertaking it; however, increasing the task's intensity causes the less capable agent to retreat, allowing the more capable agent to assume responsibility. These findings offer practical guidance for optimizing decision-making in real-world MAS deployments.

Through a case-based approach, we compare the efficiency of the most probable mixed-strategy equilibrium against two pure-strategy equilibria. Furthermore, we define Pareto optimality for the single-agent context and identify the most likely equilibrium across different task difficulty distributions. Regular group actions constitute a significant and extensively studied subclass of straight actions, holding particular importance in Cartesian Decomposition (CD). Historically, the analysis of finite regular actions and their fixed-point structures has predominantly followed a case-by-case approach. This paper takes a distinct geometric and algebraic trajectory. We begin by synthesizing existing knowledge into a coherent framework, subsequently identifying new algebraic invariants that serve as the foundation for a comprehensive classification of all non-abelian simple diagonal groups acting regularly on Cartesian decompositions. Consequently, we establish a complete list of ten primitive rank 3 actions associated with these diagonal groups. Finally, we detail the structural properties of the coverings of their Cartesian products, incorporating specific geometric configurations. The findings presented here lay the groundwork for a full classification of all non-abelian simple groups acting on non-trivial Cartesian decompositions. As an application, we derive a strengthened version of the theorem by K. Maga and R. Strobl [18], which establishes that almost all coverings of the product of two identical coverings are trivial.
Sloshing-Sagnac interferometers (SSI) offer a compelling alternative to conventional interferometer configurations for high-sensitivity rotation sensing. In this setup, sensitivity scales favorably with total power utilized in the system rather than the limiting available source power. Furthermore, sloshing motion introduces favorable time-correlated noise that enhances sensitivity beyond the standard quantum limit. However, practical applications are constrained by the sloshing frequency and the physical volume of the fluid. This study experimentally tests a gas-filled SSI, utilizing helium as the working medium to achieve a high sloshing frequency while minimizing required volume. We outline the key components necessary for optimal sensitivity and the influence of various noise sources, ultimately predicting the optimal sloshing frequency under specific conditions. The results indicate that system volume significantly impacts sensitivity; specifically, a tenfold reduction in volume could degrade sensitivity by approximately twentydecibels. Despite these limitations, the sloshing action enables significant gains in noise level at the cutoff frequency. For instance, with a volume of 100mL, a helium fill pressure of 5bar, and mW of optical power, we observed an 80decibel reduction in noise at 1Hz relative to the 10Hz reference frequency. These findings suggest that further optimizations in volume, fill pressure, and total optical power could make SSIs effective rotation sensors capable of detecting Taro rotation. Additionally, the experiment serves to validate theoretical models across a broad frequency range, from 1Hz to 10kHz.
Large-scale multiple-access XL-MIMO systems deploy massive arrays of antenna units (AUs) to cover wide service areas, extending the channel coherence time and range without increasing per-AU computational loads or power consumption. This architecture offers significant advantages for wide-area coverage, enhanced energy efficiency, and reduced land use. However, user equipment (EU) range limitations and deep fading in distant AU regions can degrade random access (RA) performance and cause resource waste. To address this, we introduce NOVR-XL, a non-orthogonal RA protocol for XL-MIMO that leverages the large coherence range to improve access performance across all AUs. Simulations based on a system with 100 AUs demonstrate that NOVR-XL achieves up to 100x better access throughput than conventional orthogonal RA methods (specifically TIME-division and CODED-division approaches), while maintaining identical access throughput and delay for a given distribution of target users. We further develop NOVR-XL with extended training sequences (NOVR-XL-RP) and optimize its parameters through machine learning (NOVR-OPT). Finally, we develop a full-system solution named SYSTEM-XL, which dynamically selects access protocols and schedules resources to maximize access throughput. Simulations confirm that SYSTEM-XL significantly outperforms existing solutions like NOVR-L (designed for conventional XL-MIMO systems), TIME-XL, and CODED-XL in access throughput, with improvements reaching 3x over NOVR-L and 10x over TIME-XL and CODED-XL. To enable practical deployment of REAL-XL systems, we conclude by discussing key design considerations and challenges related to channel estimation, user scheduling, and access throughput optimization. Neural language models are recognized for their superior performance in various natural language processing applications, including machine translation and textual entropy reduction. Although standalone neural models have achieved significant success, hybrid systems that integrate traditional $N$-gram models with neural networks have historically been underutilized. This paper demonstrates that $N$-gram models serve as effective regularizers during the training of neural components. We conduct extensive experiments using the ICSI Meeting Transcript dataset to compare various combinations of $N$-gram and neural models as both independent systems and within hybrid frameworks. The results of these experiments indicate that training a neural model without an associated $N$-gram component yields the lowest perplexity. Conversely, incorporating an $N$-gram model alongside the neural network in a competitive setup leads to the highest quality output. Finally, these findings were validated across two distinct datasets: the MTI Chinese-English dataset and the ICSI dataset.
This research presents an hybrid optical character recognition (H-OCR) system designed to convert vote counts from English, Hindi, and regional languages into a bar graph for real-time vote tabulation and live display. The system integrates a deep learning-based OCR with a spell correction algorithm. Initially, raw OCR output is processed through the spell correction module, which leverages context to amend errors, ensuring accurate numerical and textual representation in a string format. Subsequently, these refined counts are visualized as a bar graph via live streaming. The underlying spell correction model combines n-gram based phonetic matching with neural networks. Evaluations conducted on real-time field data from the 'Parivartan' campaign demonstrate that the H-OCR significantly improves accuracy over standard OCR methods. In English and Hindi, the system reduced errors by 83.03% and 71.09%, respectively, while analyses of live streaming feedback indicated an 80% decrease in complaints regarding vote count accuracy. The source code for H-OCR is accessible at https://github.com/VivekKushwaha/OCR and the live voting platform is available at https://vote.parivartancampain.org/. Keywoards: Vote Tabulation, OCR, Spell Correction, Real Time Streaming, Live Streaming.
This study investigates an Earth-like atmosphere to identify baroclinic storms and examine their fundamental characteristics and implied dynamics. These events emerge from a simplified, yet realistic, terrestrial atmosphere constrained by an ice cap at the poles. The resulting baroclinic storms exhibit behaviors on Mars that align with previously documented phenomena. These dynamics are most intense when the contrast between the warm, airless equatorial zone and the cold, ice-covered poles is most pronounced. Such conditions typically occur early in planetary evolution following the cessation of stellar XUV radiation. These findings suggest that large-scale vortex storms manifest under these specific thermal dynamics, independent of the specific planetary parameters chosen. Such vortex dynamics have previously been observed in 3D simulations of Mars's atmosphere under even more extreme conditions, featuring thicker, denser air and stronger XUV radiation. Under these circumstances, convection plays a more significant role, often coexisting with baroclinic dynamics. In contrast, low-gravity planets with warmer, denser atmospheres experience these dynamics on synoptic scales, similar to Earth. Ultimately, these findings indicate that baroclinic eddies and vortices arise when radiative cooling dominates over convective processes, particularly in the presence of significant latent heat release during condensation within deep, dense atmospheres, or in the unique conditions found on Mars. This framework is particularly relevant for the study of dynamical Bruno functions. Leveraging this generalized Lyapunov exponent, we demonstrate that for an irreducible Bruno function $f$, the exponent remains strictly negative along all trajectories within the centralizer of $f$. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of a specific sequence of functions, which are derived from the graphs of iterates of $f$ and Lyapunov exponents, to a function that is both irreducible and convex. Finally, utilizing this convergent sequence alongside a Lyapunov map, we prove that the image of the centralizer of $f$ in $P(\mathcal{H})$ (where $\mathcal{H}$ denotes the Carathéodory domain associated with $f$) is compact. As a direct consequence, we conclude that the centralizer of $f$ in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{H})$ is compact as well. The significance of this compactness lies in its role as a prerequisite for proving that the boundary of the centralizer $\mathcal{H}_c$ exhibits Hölder continuity. Ultimately, we utilize the compactness of the centralizer's image in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{H})$, combined with the Hölder continuity of $\partial \mathcal{H}_c$, to demonstrate the Hölder continuity of the Lyapunov exponent defined over the centralizer. As an application of these findings, we show that the Lyapunov exponent for dynamical Bruno functions aligns with that of irreducible convex dynamical systems. Additionally, utilizing the Hölder continuity of the Lyapunov exponent, we address a query posed by Birnir, Ghignone, and Pfaltzgraff regarding the smoothness of the set of points where the derivative of $f$ has absolute value one.

We introduce a novel bound for the convergence rate of the Nested Neumann algorithm that addresses large inception depths, offering a significant improvement over existing bounds which are valid only for small inception depths. Numerical experiments confirm that our new bound more accurately reflects the actual convergence rate when the inception depth is small. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Nested Neumann algorithm remains effective even when the inception depth is large, provided the Neumann step's convergence rate is small and the problem's angle of incidence is not excessively close to $\pi/2$. Finally, we introduce a variant of the algorithm capable of handling matrices with complex entries, and we utilize this variant to solve a complex inclusion problem.
We address the fundamental information needs required for optimization and decision-making in contextual linear bandits. By utilizing a nonparametric context distribution to model context sequences and limiting communication to a bit string sent from the agent to the optimizer, we derive an upper bound on this bit string. This approach represents the context distribution through a set of data points. Consequently, for specific context distributions with concentrated knowledge, our method offers a significant improvement over previous techniques that have relied on uniform distributions. Furthermore, we extend this technique to solve the same problem over a kernel regression distribution, demonstrating that for uniform grids, the bit requirement scales as $d \log U$, where $U$ represents the grid's maximum coordinate. Numerical experiments confirm that our method is applicable even when contexts exist in high-dimensional spaces. Additionally, we decouple this approach from the sequence length to derive a new upper bound for a uniform distribution on a compact set. Finally, we adapt the method to a setting with an unknown context distribution, providing an upper bound that depends polynomially on the reproduction kernel Hilbert space dimension $d$ and the statistical precision $n$, the sequence length. These contributions collectively enable the application of this approach across diverse distributions, potentially benefiting online learning applications involving images, texts, or geographical locations. Our work suggests that exploiting the context distribution, whether uniform or not, represents a viable strategy. To facilitate this, we develop a novel method for encoding the context distribution into a bit string, which we incorporate into an "optimize-learn" framework. Specifically, we split this framework into an initial encoding phase and a subsequent online learning phase. Additionally, we establish tightness for our bound on the bit string used to describe the context distribution for uniform grids. The paper also provides an upper bound for a uniform grid distribution within the "learn-optimize" framework and details a construction for a nearly tight distribution in this context. Lastly, we apply this construction to a contextual linear bandit problem to demonstrate its effectiveness. Our findings indicate that for fixed sequences of contexts $X_1, ..., X_n$, the growth of the bit requirement $b_n$ on a uniform grid is minimal. Conversely, for uniform distributions over continuous sets, our bound suggests that $b_n$ grows slowly with $n$, warranting further investigation into the tightness of this bound for such sets in the "optimize-learn" framework. Ultimately, the utilization of the context distribution on a discrete set constitutes a valid distribution-exploitation technique.
We present a 3D radiative transfer (RT) model specifically designed for low-density, dusty disks outside the dust optical depth of one. This model functions as a standalone cooling module that can be easily integrated into hydrodynamical simulations. By employing an optimized P^1-flux method, we ensure the solution remains robust even in the presence of intense RT sources in low-optical-depth environments. We have validated our approach using a set of standard test cases. Employing this efficient cooling model, we conducted a series of simulations with active thermodynamics in large, outer-region, low-density protoplanetary disks containing non-negligible dust fractions. These simulations demonstrate that dust significantly enhances cooling, allowing temperatures to drop by over two orders of magnitude in the disk's center. Furthermore, we developed a simplified cooling model based on our RT model to facilitate the investigation of hydrodynamical phenomena in these massive, dusty disks. However, we find that this simplified model yields inaccurate results at dust fractions exceeding ten percent, highlighting the necessity for the rigorous RT model in such environments. To address the challenge of efficient cooling in inner regions where dust is abundant, we propose utilizing a heat sink mechanism, analogous to that used in accretion disks. Ultimately, this study confirms that thermodynamics play a crucial role in determining the hydrodynamical evolution of protoplanetary disks, emphasizing that future hydrodynamical investigations must incorporate realistic cooling models. Our recommended configuration for a comprehensive thermal model is a P_N radiative transfer approach for the outer regions and a heat sink mechanism for the inner regions. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/abenoit15/RACTCOOL.

This research investigates a random walk method designed to mitigate communication inefficiencies in model learning from distributed datasets. The approach utilizes local datasets to construct random walk models via gradient descent without transmitting the original data. To further reduce communication loads, periodic updates to these models occur through the random walk strategy; during this process, only concise update information is sent from clients to the server for aggregation, rather than detailed gradient data. Our findings indicate that this technique effectively converges to accurate global models while minimizing communication overhead. Additionally, the method offers privacy advantages by limiting information exposure during learning. Furthermore, it is applicable to various optimization algorithms, including stochastic gradient descent, coordinate descent, and proximal gradient descent. Regarding privacy, we demonstrate that adding Gaussian noise to the random walk update information protects against inference attacks, ensuring data confidentiality. Simulations conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that the random walk approach successfully replaces traditional strategies like split coordinate descent and coordinate descent with thresholding. The study also reveals a trade-off between convergence speed and the noise level in update information, with simulations suggesting a power-law relationship among communication cost, noise level, and convergence rate. Finally, the method's flexibility allows for the incorporation of encryption techniques to enhance privacy further.
Although regularization techniques like label smoothing and interpolation-based mixing have been widely used in semi-supervised learning (SSL) for medical image segmentation, there remains a gap in understanding their function as regularization strategies within this specific application. This study systematically investigates the hyperparameter settings for an interpolation-based mixing method, considered one of the most effective SSL regularization approaches, across a range of medical image segmentation tasks. We begin by deriving a closed-form equation to replace the iterative interpolation-based mixing process, which we term Direct Direct Supervision (DDS). By substituting iterative mixing with DDS, computational resources can be reallocated to optimize other hyperparameters. This reallocation, combined with the systematic examination of regularization strength and data proportionality, enables the precise identification of optimal configurations. Experimental results indicate that the DDS approach, when utilizing a regularization strength higher than previously employed, consistently outperforms conventional methods. Furthermore, the new method achieves performance comparable to a recent cutting-edge iterative interpolation-based mixing technique. These findings underscore the value of exploring regularization techniques at regularization levels exceeding current standards. To facilitate future research, the source code for this approach is accessible at: https://github.com/mohammadreza99/MedSegSSL.

These same nonlocal properties form the basis for nonlocal quantum steering, which occurs when a single-photon state is combined with an auxiliary quantum system, enabling nonlocal steering of that auxiliary system. We examine these nonlocal features through the lens of single-particle steering and particle-wave duality. Furthermore, we extend these concepts to a scenario involving two distinct single-particle systems, which we then apply to create a quantum switch that sequences photonic paths. In this switch configuration, we demonstrate single-particle entanglement between previously uncorrelated photons traversing different path-dependent systems. Ultimately, we conclude that single-particle entanglement serves as a vital resource for generating nonlocality in particle-wave and particle-particle scenarios. Additionally, we highlight the significance of quantum interference and coherence in establishing these nonlocal correlations. To facilitate this research, we develop a mathematical framework based on first-order density operators acting on symmetrized tensor products of Hilbert spaces, an approach that differs from traditional methods that utilize higher-order density operators to describe single-particle entanglement. Furthermore, it addresses criticisms regarding the reality of single-particle entanglement found in ref. {steck_critic}, as well as concerns raised in ref {sougato_crit} concerning the nonlocality of quantum switches. Deepfake audio and video forgeries, alongside other information breaches, pose significant threats to the security and privacy of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) systems. Integrating Blockchain technology with IoV offers a potential solution to mitigate data loss, fake data issues, and related problems. This paper introduces a novel Lightweight Authentication and Data Sharing Protocol based on Blockchain for IoV, termed BL-EDLP. The protocol ensures data confidentiality, maintains system availability, and utilizes Distributed Ledger Technology to resolve data authenticity concerns by establishing data immutability. A mathematical analysis confirms the protocol's resistance to known attacks, while simulations using the Blockchain simulator Chaincode Developer Demonstrate (CCDX) validate the proposed distributed ledger's efficiency. Collectively, the theoretical framework, security proofs, and simulation results demonstrate that BL-EDLP effectively addresses security and privacy challenges in IoV, with potential applications in other distributed system architectures. The key contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
1.  A Blockchain-based architecture is designed to ensure data immutability in IoV, leveraging its decentralized nature to eliminate single points of failure and enhance data availability.
2.  A protocol is proposed that incorporates encryption, Digital Signature Technology, and Blockchain Technology to address security and privacy issues within IoV systems.
3.  The advantages of integrating Blockchain with IoV are analyzed, and potential challenges in this integration are discussed.
4.  The specific roles of Smart Contracts and Distributed Ledgers are discussed in the context of IoV.
5.  Simulation of the distributed ledger's efficiency is performed using the Chaincode Developer Demon (CCCD) framework.
6.  An economic analysis is conducted to assess the cost-effectiveness of adopting Blockchain technology in IoV systems.
7.  Future research directions regarding this integration are identified and discussed.
This study introduces a novel hybrid deep learning architecture, combining a Factorized Fast Transformer (FFT) with an LSTM, termed FDHT-LSTM, to enhance throughput and energy efficiency for audio recognition tasks without sacrificing accuracy. The FFT component replaces the computationally heavy original tensor decomposed (TDC) models, while the LSTM remains unchanged to ensure compatibility with existing hardware deployments. Extensive experiments comparing FDHT-LSTM against the conventional TTC-Hardware model confirm that our architecture delivers superior throughput and energy efficiency. Specifically, deployment results on an FPGA show that a 20x compressed 10-class LSTM model achieved a 2.6x increase in throughput and a 3.7x improvement in energy efficiency. Similarly, a 40x compressed 5-class Convo5-LSTM model demonstrated a 1.9x rise in throughput and a 2.6x gain in energy efficiency. Furthermore, the FDHT-LSTM hardware design requires smaller footprints, lower wire congestion, and reduced area compared to the traditional TTC-Hardware approach. The proposed architecture and its implementation specifications are available at https://github.com/sembaruthi/FDHT-LSTM.
This paper examines the Bateman-Horn conjecture within the realm of function fields. We establish an equidistribution result for polynomial splits in field extensions—an counterpart to Chebotarev's density theorem—and utilize this to derive an asymptotic formula serving as the primary ingredient for a proof of the Bateman-Horn conjecture. Furthermore, we discuss potential generalizations of this work to Artin-Langlands parameters and angular momentum distributions. As applications, we derive Chebotarev-like equidistribution results for families of automorphic forms over function fields, and we investigate the Kida relation, a conjecture concerning Fermat-Chebotarev asymptotics for pairs of Hilbert-Poincaré series satisfying the Tchebotareff property. These applications highlight areas where an asymptotic theory for angular momentum distributions over function fields could yield significant insights. Finally, we address why such a theory has not yet been developed. As a byproduct, we derive an asymptotic version of the multiplicative equidistribution of residue polynomials, an result with potential significance for number theory. These side findings also serve as a demonstration of how probabilistic methods can address problems traditionally associated with analytic number theory, particularly concerning singular series. As an illustration, we utilize this approach to rederive the circular system of laws for traces of Frobenius, a result with connections to the Chebyshev bias and Artie's conjecture. In the process, we also obtain an asymptotic formula for the number of monic irreducible polynomials taking square values. Additionally, the probabilistic framework employed here may find utility in other contexts, such as proving that, for hyperelliptic curves over $\mathbb{F}_q$, the rank of the associated Jacobian is equidistributed modulo 2, an result linked to Chebotarev's density theorem for these curves.
This paper addresses the fundamental issue of blow-up behavior in Schrödinger solutions that encounter a boundary. We demonstrate that standard classical proof methods are hindered by the presence of a boundary and propose an alternative approach yielding a novel result. Utilizing a probabilistic method, we show that for $p < p_c(\Omega)$, where $p_c(\Omega)$ depends on the boundary $\partial\Omega$, there exists a blow-up solution to the Schrödinger equation with the nonlinearity power equal to the dimensional critical exponent. Furthermore, by employing a limiting process, we establish the existence of blow-up solutions for any nonlinearity power strictly below the conformal critical exponent in the case where the boundary is absent. Our existence proof for the boundary scenario relies on a novel construction of initial data near the boundary, distinct from traditional techniques; consequently, our result does not constitute a direct generalization of the standard theorem to settings with boundaries. The analysis suggests that the set of blow-up solutions for Schrödinger equations with boundaries is likely restricted to nonlinearity powers below the critical exponent dependent on the geometry of $\partial\Omega$. To investigate the global dynamics of these solutions, we propose several open questions regarding the Schrödinger equation with boundaries. Our study highlights that boundary conditions significantly influence the dynamics of wave-like phenomena, a factor that must be considered in applications involving boundaries. Our methodology incorporates geometric optics near the boundary combined with probabilistic techniques, offering a framework applicable to other partial differential equations where boundary conditions play a crucial role. In this work, we consider the cubic nonlinearity $|u|^{p-1}u$ with $p=3$ and the Neumann boundary condition $\partial_u/\partial\nu = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$. Our findings indicate that, under these conditions, global existence holds for any initial data $u_0 \in H^1(\Omega)$. Specifically, if $u(t,x)$ represents a blow-up solution, then its initial data $u_0$ must exhibit negative energy.
In commutative algebra, lifting phenomena occur when algebraic structures from a quotient $A/I$ are elevated to $A$. We examine classic lifting issues in commutative algebra and operator theory, focusing on the distinction between positive and zero characteristic. Specifically, we analyze how these characteristics influence lifting behavior. While lifting is possible in the positive-characteristic setting, we demonstrate that no universal lifting theorem exists for zero characteristic. However, by incorporating additional hypotheses, we establish a lifting result for zero characteristic that parallels the approach used in the positive characteristic. Furthermore, we explore the connection between these phenomena and Chevalley's theorem on the structure of abelian varieties over finite fields. Regarding operator theory, we define and investigate matrix and operator variants of these phenomena, clarifying existing literature and extending the concepts to infinite-dimensional operators. Our study confirms that a Chevalley-style decomposition theorem can be formulated for normal operators, which we subsequently apply to split hyponormal and semi-hyponormal operators. Finally, we formulate an analog of this decomposition theorem for arbitrary operators, ensuring the decomposition components align with those in the Chevalley theorem. To achieve this, we also define and examine the necessary spectral idempotents, an extension of the trace theorem mentioned earlier. Ultimately, we establish an Frobenius-style theorem as an corollory to the Chevalley decomposition theorem for normal operators; similarly, we formulate Frobenius-style results for matrix and matrix-like structures, as well as for operators, contingent upon the validity of Chevalley-type decomposition theorems for those specific operators. To facilitate this research, we also preliminarily define and discuss various related concepts.
Hypothesis selection represents a fundamental decision-theoretic challenge across numerous applied domains. This paper introduces a novel framework for variable priority multistage decision theory tailored to hypothesis selection tasks. We begin by defining a utility function that reflects the goals inherent in hypothesis selection and integrates the variable importance structure specific to each problem instance. Leveraging this utility function, we develop an efficient algorithm for computing the optimal policy and demonstrate its scalability through a criminal justice use case, where we analyze the resulting utility function and value function to offer insights that support better decision-making. To incorporate stakeholder preferences into this preference elicitation process, we adapt an algorithm typically used in game theory, introducing for the first time the concept of a utility table for hypothesis selection problems. As the algorithm traces the optimization process, we explain how to populate this utility table to ultimately optimize the original utility function. As a special application, we consider a five-point Likert scale commonly used to quantify utility preferences. Finally, we conclude by discussing potential future research directions. The associated code is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/soumyadeepo/VariablePriorityHypothesisSelection. Key related terms include belief functions, criminal justice, decision theory, optimization, and utility theory.
We present DiscSense, a comprehensive new discourse annotation framework that integrates both semantic relations and the evaluation of discourse markers (DMs). This dataset includes 2,000 sentences with detailed semantic relation annotations and their confidence levels (a discourse semantic relation confidence interval), covering a diverse range of relations from simple additivity to complex adversarial structures, all labeled with an appropriate two-argument relation type and a specific DM. Additionally, DiscSense serves as a resource for training AI systems and algorithms to enhance their ability to infer semantic relations between sentence pairs. To facilitate this, we have made the dataset publicly available at https://github.com/lucrezia-torresinelli/DiscSense. In this paper, we also develop algorithms tailored for a statistical model of semantic relation confidence intervals conditioned on the co-occurrence of sentence pairs and discourse marker types. Utilizing DiscSense, we train a statistical classifier based on pair-type-marker type co-occurrences to estimate an interval of confidence for an independent test set. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical application of DiscSense for manually validating semantic relations in the wild using the public instance-based subset. Finally, we highlight the benefits of datasets like DiscSense for training artificial intelligence systems, including large language models, to infer semantic relations between sentence pairs.
We introduce a Jordanian twist within the generalized framework established by Jayewardene and Zhang, applying this to the twisted Yangian $Y(\mathfrak{g},\theta)$ associated with a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ and an involution $\theta$. When the underlying vector space is the vector representation $V=\mathbb{C}^d$, the corresponding $R$-matrix aligns with that of the simpler Jordanian twist. Consequently, the deformed $Y(\mathfrak{g},\theta)^{\otimes d}$-module $V^{\otimes d}$ retains a rich structural complexity. Furthermore, if $\mathfrak{g}= \mathfrak{sl}_n$ and $n=d+1$, we demonstrate that this specialized deformation reconnects to the $T\!V_n$-structure developed by Beattie, Le, and Schroder. Finally, for the affine type $A_1$ case, i.e., $\mathfrak{g}= \widehat{\mathfrak{sl}_1}$, the framework comprehends a recently defined deformed $specialized$ trigonometric R-matrix proposed by Beattie.
This paper presents a novel, completely symbolic decision procedure for determining whether the containment of one unlabelled regular expression within another is decidable. The approach extends Brzozowski's operator, which parameterizes a decision theory for regular expression containment, by defining a set of transformations applicable to a regular expression tree (RET) representation of the expression. These transformations include symmetrization, quotienting, and idempotency. The procedure concludes with one of three potential optimizations: minimization, conversion to deterministic finite automata (DFA), or retention as an advanced RET. We implemented this strategy in the software tool SYRUP and evaluated it using a set of regular expressions sourced from two toolsets and two academic papers. Evaluation logs demonstrate the sequence of transformations applied during each query. Our implementation has not been optimized for speed; nonetheless, it achieves success on queries that fail in suboptimal toolsets like GRAMPS and RE, which are limited to a restricted set of expressible operators. Furthermore, the decision process offers transparency by making each step visible, a feature particularly valuable for regular expressions of high complexity or those used in non-trivial evaluations. Ultimately, our method provides an explicit, step-by-step derivation of containment decisions, enhancing understanding of the relationships between expressions in a set. This work gratitude supports by constructing a symbolic decision procedure for regular expression containment (RXC) that builds upon Brzozowski's operator and is utilized here for the first time to analyze the operator set of the symbolic expression toolset SYRUP. Keyword: Regular Expression, Syntax Highlighting, Brzozowski's Operator, Symbolic Computation, SYRUP Toolset. The regular expression (RE) operator set defined in [6] (adapted from [2]) includes: Concatenation, Union (implemented via Kleene Plus for clarity), Closure (Kleene Star), Character Class, Shorthand Character Class, Range, Complement, Anchors, and Character Predicates. Although our decision strategy (outlined below) is theoretically applicable to any RE set, its practical implementation has been restricted to the SYRUP toolset (and similarly for SYOR), which supports a subset of the full operator set. These limitations exist solely for implementation purposes and do not impact the generality of our approach. Furthermore, as demonstrated in [6], these restrictions are unnecessary when employing RET representations, a fact we leverage in the implementation described herein. In the following sections, we detail our decision procedure, its implementation, and the results of its evaluation.

This study introduces a novel calibration technique for lobster-eye optics (LEO) based on a simple cross-shaped source. By analyzing the segments of the "crab-eye" image produced by the LEO system, the system's azimuthal rotation angle is determined. The calibration begins with an rough estimate using a low-resolution LEW (LEO wide-field) image to locate the four segments of the cross source as they appear within the "crab-eye" view. Once these segments are identified, the precise rotation angle of the cross source relative to the LEO is calculated. This method was successfully applied to the LEW on the lobster-eye imager (LI) aboard the Chinese satellite YaGuN-1, allowing for rapid and simple calibration of the LEW segment cameras. Consequently, the cross source serves as an effective tool for both initial alignment and ongoing monitoring of on-orbit calibration. Furthermore, this approach offers a straightforward solution for calibrating LEO systems that lack built-in radiation sources. The findings indicate that the cross source is an ideal reference for quick calibration before observing transient events. In addition, this simple source facilitates the detection of misaligned micro lenses within the LEO array, enabling their exclusion from scientific data analysis. Finally, the cross source facilitates the study of point-source imaging resolution across the entire field of view and supports the creation of a resolution map for the system.
Despite the success of density-only neural networks in reconstructing dark matter halos and merging events from cosmological simulation data, they fall short when predicting halo masses for low-abundance structures. In this study, we investigate cosmological simulations defined by the $\Lambda$CDN parameter set, which aligns closely with current observational constraints. Initially, we analyze the rank-2 spectrum of the Jacobian matrix for a subset of simulations with a relatively high amplitude of initial scalar perturbations ($n_s=0.95$, $A_s=2\times10^{-2}$), a scenario unlikely to reflect real-world conditions. This examination reveals a distinct transition in the number of non-negative eigenvalues, a shift directly correlated with the complexity of the field distributions. Subsequently, we evaluate a "density-only" network architecture on simulations with lower complexity ($A_s=2\times10^{-4}$), utilizing image, voxel, and point-cloud inputs. When predicting halo masses from voxel and point-cloud data, the model achieves nearly identical results, a finding we extend to a "volume-only" representation. Finally, we compare these outcomes with a model informed by full simulation data (density, velocity, and position), which serves as the baseline for all previous voxel-based analyses.
Atomic interferometry represents the most sensitive detection method for local magnetic fields, achieving sensitivity within an atomic wavelength. This study employs an atomic interferometer to measure the decay of local fields generated by a magnetized permanent bar. We confirm that these fields persist at a nanotesla scale (10 nT) approximately 10 cm from the bar and at a picotesla scale (100 pT) about 3 meters away. These results validate the existence of local magnetic fields in atomic interferometry and verify that our setup is sufficiently sensitive to identify minor sources of magnetism, such as those found in the pickup loops, cables, and the magnet itself, which could otherwise introduce spurious signals. Furthermore, we directly verify the vector nature of the magnetic field by detecting its rotation around the bar, a phenomenon previously unobserved in atomic interferometry. Additionally, these measurements allow us to characterize the2D cross-sectional geometry of the local field lines, providing additional insights into the magnetic properties of the permanent bar. Finally, the ability to directly detect and quantify these fields enables the neutral-atom community to further optimize and characterize their setups, a critical step for reaching the highest levels of sensitivity. To facilitate this, we provide a set of recommendations for characterizing local magnetic fields, which may also be applicable to other areas of cold-atom research where such fields are a concern. Complementary to these recommendations, we develop a simplified model to guide the community in estimating the sensitivity required to detect a specific local field at a given distance, considering the overall experimental configuration. This model is implemented as a Python script available at https://github.com/NIST-AI/Magnetic-Field-Characterization.

Although deep learning achieves high accuracy in image classification, these models often fail when dealing with imbalanced datasets, a common challenge in real-world applications. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and ensemble classifiers have been widely used to improve network performance on such datasets. This study examines the impact of combining CNNs with multiple voting-based ensemble classifiers on the performance of an underrepresented heart disease dataset. The network's performance was assessed using ten algorithms: five standard CNN variants and five ensemble configurations built upon those base networks. Results show that both the baseline CNN and the ensemble approaches significantly outperformed the traditional SVM, DsVM, and FoxCVX support vector machine variants. Specifically, the CNN-based ensemble methods achieved a K-Fold Cross-Validation (KFCV) F1-score of 0.89 and accuracy of 0.88. Furthermore, the proposed three-fold ensemble CNN (3FECNN) surpassed all other ensemble variants, delivering a F1-score of 0.90 and an accuracy of 0.89 on the underrepresented dataset. These findings confirm that utilizing ensemble classifiers to optimize CNNs significantly enhances overall model performance. The source code for this research is accessible at https://github.com/AbdulWahed/UnderNetWork.
At high energies, the parton distribution function (PDF) for a hadron turning into a vector boson $V$ ($q(x)$) exhibits a logarithmic rise as $x$ approaches unity. Recently, a universal cutoff was proposed to restrain this growth and ensure the finiteness of scattering amplitudes at infinite energy for fixed longitudinal momenta. This cutoff induces substantial corrections to conventional perturbative QCD practices, particularly for processes like same-sign $WW$ and neutral-current/di-boson ($XX$, where $X=Z,\gamma^*$, or heavy $VV$) production and multi-boson scattering. In this study, we demonstrate that these "finite energy" or "same energy" corrections vanish in the limit of high center-of-mass energy ($\sqrt{s}$) for fixed fractional energies $x_1,x_2$ or total momenta $p_z$. Consequently, these corrections represent an artifact of combining fixed-order perturbative QCD with fixed-energy constraints. We find that these "finite energy" corrections compete with $1/s$ power suppressions typically associated with "high energy" effects, such as angle suppression in scattering. Consequently, phenomena like multi-boson scattering often misinterpreted as high-energy features (e.g., resonances, extra vectors, composite nature, or dark sector particles) could actually stem from these fixed-energy fixed-order effects. To clarify this distinction, we introduce a unified regularization method applicable to both high-energy and fixed-order scenarios. Using this approach, we provide finite, positive definite predictions for same-sign $WW$ production (both charged and neutral) at the LHC and future colliders like the HL-LHC and FCC-hh. Similarly, we analyze the Drell-Yan process ($XX$), emphasizing the need for precise measurements of this process at lower masses to discover new heavy vector bosons ($VV$) at future colliders. We also estimate the impact of these corrections on direct dark photon searches. As an application of our "high energy" regularization method (often called a soft-collinear effective theory (SCET) matching method), we calculate leading power (LP) differential cross sections using a junction regularization scheme for the PDF, enabling precise analyses of angular distributions in multi-boson scattering. This precision is crucial for finding new physics signals at higher mass scales than currently accessible. Tarski's incompleteness has long served as the more precise formulation of Godel's first incompleteness phenomenon. In 1941, Rosser enhanced Godel's original proof by introducing a specific sentence, now known as the Rosser sentence. While Godel's phenomenon stems from the coexistence of an undecidable sentence and its negation within a formal system, Tarski's result arises from the undecidability of an infinite sequence of sentences, a distinction I term the Tarski phenomenon. Although Godel's phenomenon has been extensively studied and strengthened, the specific implications of Tarski's phenomenon have received less attention. This paper demonstrates that, much like Godel's phenomenon, the Tarski phenomenon admits multiple manifestations. We examine these various forms and their implications, ultimately establishing a version of Godel's first incompleteness principle that directly utilizes one of these forms to yield an undecidability result for a single sentence, effectively serving as an incompleteness phenomenon tailored to the application of the Fuzzy Cognitive Map model. Additionally, we provide an constructive proof of Godel's first incompleteness principle (as found in [6]) that is amenable to computer verification, which is then employed to derive an undecidability result for a fuzzy truth value value using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps. Furthermore, we apply Godel's second incompleteness principle to demonstrate that the value fostering the undecidability of the corresponding formal sentence cannot be constructed via Godel's most basic recursive function, nor through the mu-calculation method utilized in fuzzy logic. Finally, we outline an open problem concerning the potential for Godel's second incompleteness principle to address the undecidability of the fuzzy truth value employed in our fuzzy cognitive map approach. The findings of this study suggest that Godel's first and second incompleteness phenomena, along with their various extensions and constructive proofs, hold significant relevance for fuzzy logic and its associated methodologies. These principles can serve as powerful tools for highlighting the limitations of specific mathematical techniques applied to formal systems when dealing with the undecidability of fuzzy truth values in fuzzy cognitive maps and similar concepts. In contrast to classical systems, nonlinearity and time-variancy are the primary sources of complexity in fractional-order systems; linear subspaces represent an additional layer of difficulty. This paper examines the concepts of invariance and decomposition for fractional-order systems, aiming to clarify why these ideas are less significant in such contexts. We demonstrate that, unlike in classical systems, linear subspaces are generally not invariant in fractional-order systems unless the systems operate on the integer-axis. Furthermore, we show that fractional-order systems cannot be uniquely decomposed based on invariant linear subspaces. Finally, we explore alternative definitions of linearity and invariance in the broader context of harmonic systems. The findings presented here clarify why unique decomposition along invariants linear subspaces—commonly used in classical systems to analyze controllability, observability, and dynamic modes—is not feasible for fractional-order systems. Instead, we propose a comparable approach utilizing a fractional-order relative state-space representation.
This work establishes a novel observability inequality for the biharmonic equation, incorporating a second-order local integrable boundary damping governed by the Laplacian, where the damping's support is not necessarily convex. Leveraging Carleman estimates and the compactness-uniqueness approach, we derive a stability result for an inverse problem. These findings demonstrate that the inclusion of Laplacian-based boundary damping in the homogeneous, damped, higher-order PDE yields a significant advantage over using the first-order derivative normal derivative. Furthermore, the new observability inequality highlights that local control via Laplacian boundary damping is feasible even without convexity, offering a benefit superior to derivative-based damping. Finally, the contribution of this study regarding the stability analysis of inverse problems lies in utilizing the "observability-control-stability" framework to derive stability estimates for this concept. By applying the observability inequality (which relies on Carleman estimates) directly, we achieve a more straightforward derivation of the stability estimate for the inverse problem compared to the compactness-uniqueness method. Overall, this research provides significant theoretical insights and practical applications for controlling higher-order PDEs through Laplacian boundary damping and for resolving inverse problems, particularly regarding the distinct roles of Laplacian versus derivative-based damping. The findings also suggest future possibilities for applying Carleman estimates, observability, and stability frameworks to other systems featuring Laplacian boundary damping. At high temperatures, the combined effects of thermal corrections, a minimal dark sector, and the seesaw mechanism can suppress electroweak symmetry breaking, potentially rendering the vacuum unstable and allowing dark parity symmetry to remain unbroken. This scenario leads to a stable, light vector mediator within the dark sector and implies that vacuum stability determines the theory's symmetry-breaking pattern. We examine the implications for vector and axial vector mediators, finding that vector mediators produce observable self-energy modifications in the dark sector, whereas vector and axial vector mediators both generate distinct deviations in cosmic microwave background anisotropies and ultraviolet completeness regarding global symmetries. Specifically, vector mediators indicate the existence of vector-like fermions to ensure stability, while axial vector mediators point to magics as the source of spontaneous symmetry breaking for these symmetries. Additionally, vector mediators yield a stable minimal dark sector density $\Omega_{\rm charm} \approx 0.03$, whereas axial vector mediators result in $\Omega_{\rm hidden} \approx 0.11$. Ultimately, vector mediators offer ultraviolet completion via vector meson dominance and hadronic axions, while axial vector mediators rely on the decay of heavy neutral leptons to achieve the same. These conclusions remain valid across various masses for the vector mediator and the minimal dark sector. To visualize these findings, we present a mass plane for the vector mediator and vector-like fermions that highlights the parameter space compatible with all considered ultraviolet completions and cosmological constraints.
